title: Prefix caching technical deep dive - Horizon Systems
summary: Deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy for Horizon's multi-tenant LLM use cases. Discussed cache key design, tenant isolation, hit-rate tradeoffs, TTLs, and implications for batching/quantization. Action items: run benchmark with salted keys, evaluate on-prem cache option, and share security docs and recommended config templates.
action_items: Emily Wong: run a 24h workload test with tenant-salted keys and provide hit-rate heatmap (due: 2025-09-18)
Sara Lin: provide Redwood prefix-caching config template + recommended TTLs and sample benchmark script (due: 2025-09-15)
Michael Ortega: share security whitepaper + SOC2 artifact links and schedule on-prem sizing call (due: 2025-09-14)
next_steps: Redwood to share config template and security docs
Horizon to run salted-key benchmark and share results
Schedule follow-up to discuss on-prem cache sizing and network topology
transcript:
[00:00] Michael Ortega: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're going to walk through prefix caching strategy and how it impacts latency and cost. can everyone hear me?
[00:08] Raj Patel: yeah loud and clear, thanks Michael.
[00:12] Michael Ortega: great. quick intros? Sara from our SE team will drive the technical bits.
[00:16] Sara Lin: hi all, hi, hi. sara lin, inference se, i run the caching and runtime stuff.
[00:20] Emily Wong: emily, ml eng, i'll be running the bench.
[00:22] Carlos Ruiz: carlos infra. i'm mainly concerned about network egress and on prem placement.
[00:27] Michael Ortega: perfect. agenda: hit rates, keys, multi-tenant safety, ttl, eviction, and how batching/quant interplay. we'll also touch on vpc/on-prem caching options.
[00:36] Sara Lin: okay jumping in. so prefix or prompt caching is basically storing the KV cache for repeated prefixes—common instructions, system prompts, and user history slices. we see typical win when prefixes are stable across requests.
[00:46] Emily Wong: can you define hit-rate for us relative to token reduction? like 1% hit-rate equals what cost save?
[00:52] Sara Lin: rough rule: a cache hit skips autoregressive re-compute for the cached prefix tokens, so if your average prefix is 100 tokens and you get a hit you save the cost/latency of those 100 tokens. efficiency depends on model and batching. for example on a 40B model with default kernels that's about 30-40% token cost reduction for chats with stable system prompts.
[01:12] Carlos Ruiz: is that measured per-request or per-step?
[01:15] Sara Lin: per-request: we restore the KV state up to the cached prefix. there is partial hit concept too where you can restore 50 tokens of 100. we track hit depth.
[01:23] Raj Patel: okay how do we generate keys? i'm worried about collisions and cross-tenant leakage.
[01:28] Sara Lin: good q. common approaches: full-prompt hash, prefix fingerprint, or templated key with tenant-id + prompt-hash. recommend tenant salted keys: tenant_id || salt || prompt_hash. that prevents accidental cross-tenant hits.
[01:40] Emily Wong: what about small prompt perturbations? like whitespace or punctuation changes leading to miss?
[01:45] Sara Lin: yep brittle if you use exact-hash. we recommend normalized canonicalization: strip whitespace, normalize unicode, remove tracking tokens, and optionally template variable substitution. we also support fuzzy-keying: store N-gram signatures and do top-k approximate matches —tradeoff is lookup cost and false positives.
[02:03] Michael Ortega: quick interjection — fuzzy lookups can increase CPU and memory on the cache layer. for hosted we can offload to managed redis cluster but on-prem customers often prefer local KV store.
[02:14] Carlos Ruiz: on-prem, we can't rely on your managed redis. do you support running the cache inside our VPC or even on-node?
[02:20] Sara Lin: yes two patterns: 1) sidecar per inference pod with local persistent store (rocksdb/LMDB) for low-latency restore; 2) shared tenant-scoped cache service inside VPC behind LB. sidecar gives best tail latency but higher memory footprint. shared service is easier to manage but adds network hop.
[02:36] Emily Wong: talk to me about TTLs and eviction strategy — we have skewed tenants: some get 10x traffic.
[02:43] Sara Lin: eviction policies: LRU by tenant+key, weighted by token-length and access frequency. we also support capped per-tenant quotas and admission policies — e.g., don't admit prefixes below certain reuse threshold. for skew, you can enforce per-tenant quotas so one tenant doesn't evict others.
[02:58] Raj Patel: and encryption at rest / in transit for cache?
[03:02] Michael Ortega: for hosted we encrypt in transit and at rest, keys managed with KMS. for private, the cache service can plug into your KMS/HSM, or run entirely inside customer-managed network. we'll share security docs.
[03:12] Carlos Ruiz: good. next: hit-rate expectations. emily will run a bench, but any baseline numbers?
[03:18] Sara Lin: baseline from similar customers: system prompt + role messages + last 1-2 user turns yields ~25-45% hit-rate depending on UX. some highly templated apps get 60-70%. but it depends: if users heavily personalize prompts, hit-rate drops.
[03:30] Emily Wong: how do you measure partial hits? we saw something called depth metric earlier.
[03:33] Sara Lin: depth is how many prefix tokens matched. we report hit_count, hit_depth_tokens, and effective_token_reduction. those drive cost savings.
[03:40] Raj Patel: what about consistency: if we restore cached KV and we change model weights (new model version), is cache invalidated?
[03:46] Sara Lin: yes you should key by model_version as well. we recommend key components: tenant_id, model_id+version, prompt_template_id, canonical_prompt_hash. any change in model or tokenizer invalidates that key.
[03:59] Carlos Ruiz: quantization specifics — does using INT8 or 4-bit change caching semantics?
[04:03] Sara Lin: semantics same but representation changes. quantized runtimes may have different KV memory layouts; we treat cache blobs as opaque marshalled state per runtime config. so you must ensure the cache blob was produced by same runtime kernel/quantization settings. include quantization_profile in key.
[04:18] Emily Wong: and batching — if we batch requests with different prefixes, does caching still help?
[04:22] Sara Lin: yes: batching and cached restores are complementary. you can restore different KV states for each batch item before stepping. the runtime does continuous batching after restore. the overhead is parallel restore time; set batch size to optimize throughput without inflating tail latency.
[04:35] Michael Ortega: practical tip: use adaptive batching — small batches at tail, larger in steady state. Redwood's runtime will prefer to schedule queued requests so cached restores don't block others.
[04:46] Raj Patel: can we do tenant isolation by using separate caches per tenant? pros/cons?
[04:50] Sara Lin: separate caches per tenant is strongest isolation; it's simplest for quotas and encryption. downside: memory duplication and harder to share common assets across tenants (if you want shared system prompts). a hybrid: per-tenant namespace with shared common pool for public templates but admission controls to avoid leakage.
[05:06] Emily Wong: one more: how do you avoid stale prefixes after prompt policy changes?
[05:10] Sara Lin: version your prompt templates and bake template_id into key. when prompt changes, increment template version -> auto invalidation. avoid relying on heuristics alone.
[05:19] Carlos Ruiz: network egress: if using shared cache in our VPC behind LB, what's the RTT penalty?
[05:24] Michael Ortega: typical extra 1-3ms inside cloud region if colocated; for on-prem across racks expect 5-10ms depending on topology. sidecar approach brings that to sub-ms for local NVMe-backed store.
[05:36] Raj Patel: what's Redwood's recommendation for Horizon, given our skew, strict tenancy, and plan to deploy private?
[05:42] Sara Lin: for Horizon I'd recommend: sidecar local cache per inference node for low tail latency, tenant namespaces with per-tenant quotas, canonicalization + tenant-salt in key, include model_version and quant_profile in key, and a short TTL for highly dynamic system prompts (1-6 hours) and longer TTL for stable templates (24-72 hours). run a 24h bench to capture diurnal patterns.
[06:00] Emily Wong: sounds actionable. can you explain admission policy thresholds?
[06:04] Sara Lin: we can set a reuse threshold — only admit prefixes that have been seen X times in sliding window. prevents storing one-off requests. also min token-length to avoid caching tiny prefixes.
[06:14] Raj Patel: any risk of fingerprinting users via cache timing?
[06:18] Sara Lin: possible in theory; mitigations: constant-time restore ops, rate-limit metadata endpoints, avoid per-user micro signals in shared telemetry. for high-risk apps consider per-tenant isolated caches and strict telemetry controls.
[06:31] Carlos Ruiz: will you share the cache blob format?
[06:34] Michael Ortega: we won't expose internal binary layout but we'll provide SDKs and clear marshaling APIs. for private deployments, we can include schema docs under NDA.
[06:43] Emily Wong: ok, now about metrics — what dashboards should we monitor?
[06:47] Sara Lin: hit-rate, hit_depth_tokens, restore_latency (p95), admission_reject_rate, per-tenant memory usage, eviction_rate, and token_reduction_saved. we also surface model-version mismatch errors.
[06:58] Raj Patel: if we roll out a new prompt template, how do we do canary invalidation?
[07:02] Sara Lin: you can deploy template version v2 and direct a small percent of traffic to it; its keys are separate so no cross-effect. for sweeping invalidation we recommend TTL purge by version tag.
[07:12] Michael Ortega: time check — we've covered most. any other questions?
[07:16] Emily Wong: one last: for our bench, what dataset shape will you need?
[07:20] Sara Lin: sample of user prompts with timestamps and tenant id; if possible, label templated vs freeform. and we need the current system prompt templates. we'll provide a script to convert to canonical form.
[07:30] Raj Patel: will the benchmark include quantized model configs?
[07:33] Sara Lin: yes we'll run both FP16 and INT8 profiles to show deltas. include model_version and quant_profile in your workload files.
[07:40] Carlos Ruiz: outstanding security ask: can we keep cache inside our air-gapped environment?
[07:44] Michael Ortega: yes with Redwood Private you can run the control plane optional and inference runtime plus cache entirely on-prem. we'll need to run sizing and network planning with your team.
[07:52] Emily Wong: what would sizing look like for our top tenant usage?
[07:55] Sara Lin: rough calc: average prefix size 120 tokens, average cache object size ~X KB (depends on model & quant), multiply by expected unique prefixes per tenant. sara will provide sample sizing sheet.
[08:06] Michael Ortega: okay we're getting into ops — action items again: sara will share config template, emily will run bench, michael share security docs and schedule on-prem sizing.
[08:16] Raj Patel: perfect. thanks everyone.
[51:30] Michael Ortega: wrapping — recap and we'll follow up with the docs and schedule. thanks all.
[51:40] Emily Wong: thanks, bye.
[51:42] Carlos Ruiz: thanks, bye.
[51:44] Sara Lin: bye.
